content: Scalp rashes, while often straightforward to diagnose, can present challenges in treatment. Effective management may require the use of topical therapies alone or in combination with systemic treatments over extended periods to achieve and maintain full control of the condition. Differentiating Scalp Rash from Other Diseases Scalp rashes must be carefully distinguished from other conditions that can present with similar symptoms. These include: Contact dermatitis: An inflammatory reaction caused by direct contact with an irritant or allergen. Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp: A chronic inflammatory condition characterized by painful nodules and abscesses. Discoid lupus: A chronic autoimmune condition that can cause scarring and hair loss. Kerion: A severe inflammatory response to fungal infection, often presenting as a boggy, tender mass. Psoriasis: A chronic autoimmune condition marked by thick, scaly plaques. Scalp folliculitis: Inflammation of hair follicles, often due to bacterial infection. Seborrheic dermatitis: A common condition causing flaky, white or yellowish scales. Tinea capitis: A fungal infection of the scalp, often seen in children. Diagnosis History and Symptoms Seborrheic dermatitis: This condition typically presents as diffuse, white, non-adherent scales on the scalp. Bacterial folliculitis: Diagnosis can be confirmed by examining an intact pustule on the scalp. Laboratory Findings A KOH preparation can be performed in-office to identify fungal spores within the hair shaft. Fungal cultures should be obtained from areas of kerion or scalp scaling to confirm or rule out tinea capitis. A shave biopsy should be used judiciously, as it can provide valuable information in cases of seborrheic dermatitis but is not routinely necessary. Treatment Medical Therapy Acute pharmacotherapies include: Ketoconazole Tar-based shampoos Salicylic acid shampoos Zinc pyrithione Antifungal medications Corticosteroids A first-generation cephalosporin or a tetracycline derivative, typically prescribed for 2-4 weeks to address bacterial infections. Injections Intralesional steroid injections can be used to reduce inflammation in localized areas. Systemic retinoids may be considered for severe or refractory cases. Antibiotic therapy may be necessary for bacterial infections or secondary infections complicating the primary condition.
